title: Vowel harmony and plurals
intro: Most Turkmen endings change their vowel to match the word they are added to. This is called vowel harmony, and it is the key to every ending you will learn. This unit sorts the nine vowels into groups, uses them to build the plural with *-lar* or *-ler*, and adds the words for this and that, and for a or one.

blocks.text: Turkmen has nine vowels: *a, e, ä, i, o, ö, u, ü, y*. Two questions sort them. Is the vowel made at the **front** of the mouth or at the **back**? And are the lips **rounded** or not? Say e and then a: your tongue pulls back. Say i and then ü: your lips round.
For now you only need the first question, front or back: it decides the endings in this unit. Rounding comes into play in [A1 unit 3](a1-u03).
What counts is always the **last** vowel of the word, however many come before it:
Learn the groups as two short lists. Front: *e, ä, i, ö, ü*. Back: *a, o, u, y*. The vowel *y* is a back vowel and *i* a front one, although they look alike.

Many endings have two forms, one with *a* and one with *e*. Which one a word takes depends on its last vowel: after a back vowel the ending has *a*, after a front vowel it has *e*. This is two-way harmony.

blocks.label: Two-way harmony
lines: last vowel a, o, u, y     →  ending with a
last vowel e, ä, i, ö, ü  →  ending with e

blocks.text: The plural is the first ending of this kind: *-lar* after back vowels, *-ler* after front vowels.

Harmony isn't a spelling rule laid on top of the language: it makes words easier to say, because the tongue stays in one part of the mouth. Say *öýlar* and then *öýler*, and *öýler* will feel smoother.
**Borrowed words** often mix front and back vowels: *kitap* (book) has i and then a, *mekdep* (school) has e and e, *telefon* has e and then o. They follow the same rule: only the last vowel counts.
Look at the **last** vowel, not the first: *penjire* → *penjireler*, but *ruçka* → *ruçkalar*. And the front form of the plural is spelled with *e*, never *ä*: *-ler*.
Add *-lar* or *-ler* to a noun to make it plural. The word in front of the ending doesn't change.
Notice that the colour or the description after a plural noun stays as it is: *Kitaplar täze*, not *täzeler*. Only the noun takes the plural.
Turkmen uses the plural less than English does. After a number or a word of quantity, the noun stays singular: *iki kitap* (two books), *köp kitap* (many books). Numbers come in [A1 unit 11](a1-u11).
No plural after a number: *iki kitap*, never *iki kitaplar*. The number already says there is more than one.

sections.title: This and that: bu, şu, ol, şol

blocks.text: Turkmen has four words where English has two. *bu* is this, something near you. *şu* is this right here: something you point at, or something just mentioned. *ol* is that, something farther away. *şol* is that one: something both of you already know about.

Each word works in two ways. Before a noun it never changes: *bu kitap* (this book), *bu kitaplar* (these books). On its own, as a pronoun, it has a plural: *bular*, *şular*, *olar*, *şolar*. In *olar* and *şolar*, the l of *ol* and *şol* is shared with the ending.

*Bu kitap.* on its own is a full sentence: this is a book. In *Bu kitap täze*, *bu kitap* is the subject (this book) and *täze* says what it is like: this book is new. Ask *Bu näme?* about a thing and *Bu kim?* about a person.
*ol* also means he, she or it, and *olar* means they; you will use them for people in [A1 unit 3](a1-u03).
To start, use *bu* for this and *ol* for that. Use *şol* when you mean “that one, the one we talked about”: *Şol kitap täze* (that book, the one we mentioned, is new).
*bir* is the number one, and it can also work like **a** or **an**. There is no word for **the** at all: *kitap* is a book or the book, as the context says.
Turkmen uses *bir* less often than English uses **a**. *Bu kitap* already means this is a book. Add *bir* when the number matters, or to mean “a certain one”, “some”:
When you meet *bir*, ask whether the number matters. If it does, it means **one**; if not, it means **a**, and often English doesn't need it either.

summary: Nine vowels: front *e, ä, i, ö, ü*, back *a, o, u, y*.
The last vowel of the word decides the ending: *a* after a back vowel, *e* after a front one.
The plural is *-lar* or *-ler*: *kitaplar*, *depderler*, *öýler*. Borrowed words follow their last vowel too: *telefonlar*, *mekdepler*.
No plural after a number or *köp*: *iki kitap*, *köp kitap*.
*bu* this, *şu* this right here, *ol* that, *şol* that one we know; as pronouns, *bular*, *şular*, *olar*, *şolar*.
*Bu näme?* for things, *Bu kim?* for people.
*bir* is one, and sometimes a; there is no word for the.
